---
title: "Before Lesson 1"
---

Before the theory begins, establish one reliable path from code to sound.
Install Sonic Pi 5.0.0 from [sonic-pi.net](https://sonic-pi.net/); the download
page covers macOS, Windows, Linux, and Raspberry Pi. The version number belongs
to the musical setup as much as the speakers do. A later release can change a
synth default and make two people hear different evidence from the same code.

Open Sonic Pi, paste this into an empty buffer, and press **Run**.

```{.ruby audio=""}
play 60
```

That single note is a useful dividing line. If you hear it, the program has
reached the audio output. If you do not, leave the code alone and check the
volume, selected output device, and Sonic Pi log. Changing a correct line while
diagnosing the sound path creates a second problem before the first one is
understood.

Headphones or speakers with usable bass response help throughout the course.
Part 1 compares frequencies near 200 Hz, and Part 10 builds bass lines whose
shape can disappear through small laptop speakers. Keep the level low enough
that repeated drills remain comfortable.

## Which version

Every example targets **Sonic Pi 5.0.0**. The extracted Ruby clears syntax
checks, but the manuscript has not yet received its complete runtime and
listening pass. That is why each lesson remains `draft`, and why empty audio
attributes appear where recordings will eventually go. A syntax check can read
Ruby grammar; it cannot hear a melody or confirm Sonic Pi's response to a call.

If your version differs, open **Help, About** and record the number before
adapting an example. Synth defaults, samples, and function behaviour can move
between releases. When an example parses but behaves strangely, the log tells
you what the runtime objected to, while the help pane describes the installed
API. Those two sources are more useful than guessing at the code.

## The window

Most of the work happens in three areas. **Buffers** hold code; a fresh buffer
keeps definitions and live loops from an earlier lesson out of the next one.
The **log** prints messages, notes, and errors, giving you a second account of
the performance when the sound is ambiguous. The **help** pane documents the
synths, samples, and functions available in the installed version.

On macOS, `Cmd-R` runs the buffer and `Cmd-.` stops all sound. On Windows and
Linux, use `Alt-R` and `Alt-.`. Learn the stop command before running the first
live loop.

## A first sound

The next program is a preview rather than a test. Paste it into a fresh buffer
and listen to two repetitions before trying to understand every line. Parts 0
through 3 will unpack its tempo, synth selection, array, timed playback, and
concurrent loops. For now, notice that a small amount of data can already
describe a recognisable musical surface.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

# E minor pentatonic keeps the first experiment focused on rhythm and timbre.
melody = [:e4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :d5, :b4, :a4, :g4]

live_loop :tune do
  melody.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.4
    sleep 0.25
  end
end

live_loop :bass do
  play :e2, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7, cutoff: 70
  sleep 2
end
```

After two repetitions, replace `:pluck` with `:prophet` and run the buffer again.
The pitch sequence and timing stay fixed, so the softer attack and longer body
belong to the instrument. Restore `:pluck`, replace `melody` with
`[:e4, :f4, :g4, :a4, :b4, :c5, :d5, :e5]`, and listen once more. This time the
instrument stays put while the note collection changes. Parts 2 and 5 will
explain why those new notes sit differently over the E in the bass.

Press the stop shortcut before continuing. Live loops run until stopped, even
after you move to another buffer.

## How to use the draft

Work through the lessons in order because the representation accumulates. The
event schema introduced before harmony returns in notation, transcription, and
arrangement; later examples can therefore concentrate on music instead of
rebuilding their data model. Each lesson follows a familiar arc: meet the idea,
run a complete program, isolate one change, account for what you hear, then use
the idea in a larger piece of work.

Use the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd) after making a real attempt.
Use the [glossary](appendix/glossary.qmd) to recover a term and the [Sonic Pi
cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd) to recover a call. The [sources
ledger](appendix/sources.qmd) records the provenance needed for transcription
material.

When a lesson surprises you, record the version, exact edit, log output, and what
you heard. Keep syntax failure separate from Sonic Pi runtime failure, and keep
both separate from timing trouble or disagreement with the prose. That small
discipline turns "it did not work" into evidence another person can follow. It
is also the evidence required to move a lesson from `draft` to `tested`.
